module_title: Quality Control: Ensuring Safe and Effective Fertilizer

lessons.title: Testing Compost Maturity: Simple Field Tests
lessons.body: Maturity means your compost is stable and won't harm plants. Immature compost continues to heat, robbing soil of oxygen and nitrogen. To test, first do the bag test: seal a handful of moist compost in a clear plastic bag. Leave it in a warm spot for 3 days. If it smells sour or turns slimy, it's not ready. If it smells earthy and looks the same, it's likely mature. Second, the jar test: fill a jar halfway with compost, top with water, shake, and let settle for 30 minutes. Good compost has a dark brown layer on top, a clear middle layer, and a small sediment layer. Cloudy water means immature. Third, the germination test: plant 10 radish or bean seeds in a tray of your compost, and 10 in regular soil as a control. Keep moist. After 7 days, count sprouts. If compost sprouts are less than 80% of the control, wait 2 more weeks. Fourth, the temperature test: fill a bucket with compost, cover, and check temperature daily for 3 days. If it stays above 40Â°C, it's still active. Mature compost stays below 35Â°C. Finally, the smell test: mature compost smells like forest floor, not like ammonia or rotten eggs. In Africa, where temperatures are high, compost can mature in 4-6 weeks if turned regularly. Always test before using on seedlings; mature compost is dark, crumbly, and cool. If unsure, let it cure for another 2 weeks. These simple tests save you from crop failure.

lessons.title: Avoiding Contaminants: Plastics, Chemicals, and Heavy Metals
lessons.body: Contaminants can ruin your compost and your soil. Plastics are the most common problem. Never add plastic bags, bottles, or wrappers. They don't decompose and release toxins when burned. Before composting, sort your materials. Use a fork to remove any plastic pieces. If you use municipal waste, screen it through a 1 cm mesh sieve. Chemicals like pesticides, herbicides, and bleach kill the microbes that break down compost. Don't add grass clippings from lawns treated with weed killer within 3 weeks. Don't add sawdust from treated wood, which contains arsenic or copper. Heavy metals like lead, cadmium, and mercury come from batteries, old paint, and industrial waste. These accumulate in soil and enter crops. Test your compost if you suspect contamination. Simple test kits are available from agricultural extension offices. In Africa, a common source is car batteries or electronic waste. Keep these out of your compost pile. Also avoid adding meat, dairy, and oily foods, which attract pests and create odors. If you use manure, ensure it's from animals not fed antibiotics or growth hormones. Compost contaminated with heavy metals can't be fixed; you must discard it. Prevention is key: know your inputs. Keep a separate bin for questionable materials. Train your family or workers to recognize and remove contaminants. A clean compost pile produces safe fertilizer for vegetables and fruits.

lessons.title: Managing Odors and Pests in Your Compost
lessons.body: Odors mean your compost is too wet, too compacted, or has too much nitrogen. A healthy pile smells earthy. If it smells like rotten eggs, it's anaerobic. Fix by turning the pile to add oxygen. If it smells like ammonia, add carbon-rich materials like dry leaves, straw, or sawdust. Aim for a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 25:1 to 30:1. For every bucket of green material (kitchen scraps, grass), add two buckets of brown material. Moisture should be like a wrung-out sponge. If you squeeze and water drips, it's too wet; add dry material. If it's dusty, add water. Pests like flies, rodents, and cockroaches are attracted to exposed food scraps. Bury food scraps 15 cm deep in the center of the pile. Use a closed bin with a lid. In Africa, ants can be a problem if the pile is too dry. Moisten it. For rodents, avoid adding meat, bones, or oily foods. If pests persist, sprinkle wood ash or diatomaceous earth around the pile. Turn the pile every 3-5 days to disrupt pest breeding. A well-managed pile heats up to 55-65Â°C, which kills fly eggs and pathogens. If you see maggots, add lime or turn more often. Keep the area clean; don't leave piles of fresh waste. A secure bin with a tight-fitting lid and a base of wire mesh prevents rodents from burrowing. Regularly check for signs of pests and act quickly. Odor and pest control are signs of a healthy, active compost process.

lessons.title: Moisture and Temperature Monitoring
lessons.body: Moisture and temperature are the two most important factors for fast, clean composting. Ideal moisture is 50-60%. The squeeze test: grab a handful of compost and squeeze. It should feel like a wrung-out spongeâno dripping, but damp. If it drips, add dry browns like straw or sawdust. If it crumbles, add water while turning. In dry African climates, you may need to water the pile every 2-3 days. Cover it with a tarp or banana leaves to reduce evaporation. Temperature indicates microbial activity. Use a compost thermometer with a 50 cm probe, or a long metal rod. Push it into the center of the pile. In the first week, temperature should reach 55-65Â°C. This kills weed seeds and pathogens. If it's below 40Â°C, the pile is too small or too dry. Add more material or water. If it's above 70Â°C, turn it to cool it down; extreme heat kills beneficial microbes. Turn the pile when temperature drops below 40Â°C, usually every 3-5 days. After 3-4 weeks, temperature will stabilize around 30-35Â°C, meaning it's maturing. In hot climates, compost can overheat; monitor daily. In cooler highlands, it may take longer. Keep a record of temperature and moisture each day. A simple notebook works. Adjust as needed. Proper monitoring gives you finished compost in 4-6 weeks instead of 3 months.

lessons.title: Sieving and Grading Compost for Different Uses
lessons.body: Sieving removes large chunks, stones, and contaminants, giving you uniform compost. Use a sieve with 1 cm mesh for general garden use. For finer compost for seedlings, use a 5 mm mesh. Build a simple sieve with a wooden frame and wire mesh. Wear gloves. Sieve when compost is dry to avoid clogging. Work on a tarp to catch fine material. Grade your compost into three sizes: coarse (above 1 cm), medium (5 mm to 1 cm), and fine (below 5 mm). Coarse material can be used as mulch around trees and shrubs. It suppresses weeds and retains moisture. Medium grade is perfect for mixing into soil for vegetables. Fine grade is ideal for seed starting and potting mixes. Mix fine compost with sand and soil in equal parts for seedlings. For potting, use 1 part fine compost, 1 part sand, 1 part garden soil. You can also make compost tea: soak a sack of fine compost in water for 24 hours, then use the liquid as foliar feed. Sieving also helps you catch plastic or glass. In Africa, many farmers use woven baskets as sieves. That works, but wire mesh is more durable. After sieving, store compost in sacks in a dry place. Label each grade. Use coarse for perennial crops, medium for annuals, fine for nurseries. Proper grading increases the value of your compost and ensures you use the right material for each crop.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Quality Assurance
lessons.body: Record keeping helps you track what works and prove quality to customers. Start a compost logbook. For each batch, record the date you started, materials added (type and amount), and carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. Note turning dates and temperatures. Record moisture levels. When compost is ready, note the maturity test results. Also record any problems like odors or pests and how you fixed them. This data helps you repeat success and avoid mistakes. For selling, keep a batch number and date. Buyers want to know the compost is safe and mature. You can show your log as proof. Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone. If you sell to organic certifiers, they require detailed records. Include source of materials, especially manure, to show no contaminants. Record sieving dates and grades produced. Track yields: how many sacks of fine, medium, and coarse compost from each batch. This helps you price and plan. Also record sales and customer feedback. If a customer reports poor results, check your records to see if that batch had issues. In Africa, where mobile phones are common, use apps like Google Sheets or even SMS to keep notes. Train workers to record daily. A well-kept record system builds trust and helps you improve. It turns composting from a guess into a science.

quiz.q: Which simple test uses a plastic bag to check compost maturity?
quiz.explanation: The bag test seals moist compost in a plastic bag for 3 days to check for sour smell or slime.

quiz.q: In the jar test, what does cloudy water indicate?
quiz.explanation: Cloudy water means the compost is still active and not fully mature.

quiz.q: What percentage of control sprouts should compost sprouts reach to be considered mature in a germination test?
quiz.explanation: If compost sprouts are less than 80% of the control, the compost is not ready.

quiz.q: What temperature indicates compost is still active and not mature?
quiz.explanation: Mature compost stays below 35Â°C; above 40Â°C means it is still heating.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be added to compost?
quiz.explanation: Plastics do not decompose and can release toxins.

quiz.q: What is a common source of heavy metals in compost?
quiz.explanation: Car batteries contain lead and other heavy metals that contaminate compost.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before adding grass clippings from a lawn treated with weed killer?
quiz.explanation: Weed killers can persist for weeks; wait at least 3 weeks to avoid killing compost microbes.

quiz.q: What should you do if your compost smells like rotten eggs?
quiz.explanation: Rotten egg smell means anaerobic conditions; turning adds oxygen.

quiz.q: What is the ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for compost?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 25:1 to 30:1 supports efficient microbial activity.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury food scraps to avoid pests?
quiz.explanation: Burying scraps 15 cm deep in the center of the pile discourages flies and rodents.

quiz.q: What temperature range kills pathogens and weed seeds in compost?
quiz.explanation: Temperatures of 55-65Â°C are high enough to kill most pathogens and weed seeds.

quiz.q: What is the squeeze test used to check?
quiz.explanation: The squeeze test indicates if compost has ideal moisture (like a wrung-out sponge).

quiz.q: What should you do if your compost pile is too dry?
quiz.explanation: Adding water while turning restores moisture to dry compost.

quiz.q: What tool can measure compost temperature?
quiz.explanation: A compost thermometer with a long probe reaches the center of the pile.

quiz.q: How often should you turn compost when temperature drops below 40Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 3-5 days when temperature drops reintroduces oxygen and speeds decomposition.

quiz.q: What size sieve is best for compost used in seedlings?
quiz.explanation: A 5 mm sieve produces fine compost suitable for seed starting.

quiz.q: What is coarse compost (above 1 cm) best used for?
quiz.explanation: Coarse compost works well as mulch for weed suppression and moisture retention.

quiz.q: How do you make compost tea?
options: B) Soak a sack of fine compost in water for 24 hours
D) Add compost to boiling water
quiz.explanation: Soaking fine compost in water for 24 hours extracts nutrients for foliar feed.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for compost quality?
options: B) To track what works and prove quality
quiz.explanation: Records help you repeat success, avoid mistakes, and show buyers your compost is safe.

quiz.q: What should you record about materials added to compost?
quiz.explanation: Recording type and amount helps calculate carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and track contaminants.

quiz.q: What is a sign that compost is mature according to the bag test?
quiz.explanation: Mature compost smells earthy, not sour or slimy.

quiz.q: Which material should be avoided to prevent attracting rodents?
quiz.explanation: Meat scraps attract rodents and create odors.

quiz.q: What can you add to compost to reduce odors from too much nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Adding carbon-rich materials like dry leaves balances the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for compost?
quiz.explanation: 50-60% moisture feels like a wrung-out sponge and supports microbial activity.

quiz.q: What should you do if compost temperature exceeds 70Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Turning the pile releases heat and prevents beneficial microbes from dying.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of sieving compost?
options: A) To remove large chunks and contaminants
quiz.explanation: Sieving removes stones, plastics, and large pieces, giving uniform compost.

quiz.q: Which grade of compost is best for potting mixes?
quiz.explanation: Fine compost (below 5 mm) is ideal for seed starting and potting mixes.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to keep records if you have a mobile phone?
quiz.explanation: Google Sheets or similar apps allow easy record keeping on a phone.

quiz.q: Why should you record customer feedback?
quiz.explanation: Customer feedback helps identify problems and improve compost quality.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of immature compost in the jar test?
quiz.explanation: Cloudy water indicates the compost is still active and not fully mature.
